oboe.title: Oboe
oboe.intro: If you play oboe seriously, it can be part of your college path even if you don't plan to major in music.

facts.label: Recordings due
facts.value: Often around Dec 1 of senior year

facts.label: Scholarships
facts.value: Merit awards at many music schools; need-based only at Ivies

options.title: Major in music
options.description: Apply to the college and audition for its school of music, or apply to a conservatory. Your playing carries the most weight.
options.fitsIf: You want music to be most of your day.

options.title: Double or dual degree
options.description: A music degree plus a second degree, usually over five years. Some universities partner with conservatories, such as Harvard with NEC.
options.fitsIf: You're serious about both and ready for a heavy schedule.

options.title: Major in something else and keep playing
options.description: Apply normally. Many selective colleges accept an optional arts supplement, though some review it only when the rest of your application is already strong. Once you enroll, many schools offer lessons and ensembles to non-majors.
options.fitsIf: Music is a big part of you but not your career plan.

timeline.text: Private lessons; youth orchestra, honor band or all-state; start standard repertoire.
Research schools by their oboe teacher; summer music program; practice recording.
Regular application plus music supplement; prescreens and arts supplements often due around Dec 1, some earlier.
Live or recorded auditions, usually Jan–Feb; some schools add sight-reading.
Decisions by about April 1; compare music awards with financial aid; deposit by May 1.

needs.label: A private teacher who knows college audition repertoire
Prepared pieces: a concerto or sonata, etudes, orchestral excerpts
Strong grades, since music adds to the application but doesn't replace academics

callout.title: Start with your music teacher
callout.body: Your teacher hears you play every week and knows the audition repertoire. Ask which programs fit your level before you build a list.

myths.myth: Every music school wants an oboe prescreen by Dec 1.
myths.truth: It differs by school and instrument. Some don't require one for undergraduate oboe.

myths.myth: Oboe can get me a scholarship at an Ivy.
myths.truth: Ivies give no music or merit scholarships. Aid is need-based only.

myths.myth: A music scholarship means a full ride.
myths.truth: Award sizes vary by school. A few conservatories, such as Curtis, give every student full tuition.

myths.myth: If I'm not a music major I'll have to stop playing.
myths.truth: Many colleges offer lessons and ensembles to students in any major.

myths.myth: Every music school wants a prescreen.
myths.truth: It depends on the school and the instrument. Indiana asks none from undergraduate cellists or trumpeters, and Eastman asks none from guitarists.

myths.myth: I can play whatever pieces I like.
myths.truth: Most schools list required repertoire for each instrument, such as a concerto movement, Bach and an etude.

myths.myth: An edited phone video is fine.
myths.truth: Schools ask for unedited takes. Indiana's piano page also rules out added echo or reverb.

myths.myth: If I'm not a music major I'll have to stop playing.
myths.truth: Many colleges offer lessons and ensembles to students in any major.

sports.title: Popular sports
sports.intro: If you play basketball, soccer, football, baseball, softball, volleyball, lacrosse or another sport seriously, a college coach can become part of your path. You still apply to the college the regular way.

facts.label: Paths available
facts.value: Division I & II, Division III, Ivy League, NAIA

facts.label: Scholarships
facts.value: Mostly partial; none in Division III or the Ivies

options.title: Division I or II
options.description: Coaches recruit you and can offer athletic scholarships, which are mostly partial. You must meet NCAA academic standards: 16 core courses and a minimum core GPA.
submit: Athletics aid agreement, if you're offered aid
options.fitsIf: You want to compete at a high level and can meet NCAA academic standards.

options.title: Division III or the Ivy League
options.description: No athletic scholarships. You're admitted under the same standards as other students, and Ivy coaches can get early feedback on your application from admissions.
options.fitsIf: Academics come first and you want to keep competing seriously.

options.title: NAIA
options.description: A separate association with its own eligibility rules, based on your high school grades. Schools may offer athletic and academic aid, and there are no recruiting calendar limits.
options.fitsIf: You want a chance at athletic aid outside the NCAA.

timeline.text: Take NCAA-approved core courses. For Division I, 10 of the 16 must be done before senior year.
Recruiting starts for most students. Division II coaches can contact you after June 15 before junior year. Register with the NCAA or PlayNAIA.
Ivy League coaches can get admissions feedback on your application from July 1.
Official visits, one per school. Most Division I and II sports open signing on Nov 12, 2026. Ivy likely letters can arrive from Oct 1.
Signing dates vary by sport. Ivy likely letters can arrive until March 15.

needs.label: 16 NCAA-approved core courses, if you're aiming for Division I or II
A core-course GPA of at least 2.3 for Division I or 2.2 for Division II
Registration with the NCAA Eligibility Center or PlayNAIA
Strong grades, and test scores where a college wants them, since athletes still apply like everyone else
Financial aid forms, since most athletic aid is partial

callout.title: Start with your coach
callout.body: Your high school or club coach has watched you compete and knows which levels fit you. Ask them before you start contacting college coaches.

myths.myth: A verbal commitment locks in my spot.
myths.truth: It isn't binding on you or the school. Signing an athletics aid agreement is the official commitment, and in the Ivy League only the admissions office can admit you.
Most athletic scholarships are partial, and only about 2% of high school athletes are offered one.

myths.myth: I need SAT or ACT scores to be NCAA eligible.
myths.truth: Not for Division I or II anymore, though a college may still want them for admission.

myths.myth: Division III means I don't need to register.
myths.truth: Division III doesn't certify academics, but the NCAA says incoming athletes should register to get an NCAA ID.

myths.myth: I'll sign a National Letter of Intent.
myths.truth: Division I dropped it in 2024. Scholarship athletes now sign a financial aid agreement.

evidence: If you're being recruited by an NCAA Division I or II school, transition your Profile Page account to an Academic and Athletics Certification account.

Division III student-athletes are generally held to the same admissions standards, academic standards, housing policies and support services as the general student body.
Division III schools set their own admissions and academic standards.

sources.label: NCAA Eligibility Center
